Class ListView<T>

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.AbstractPanelElement
com.trevlar.menukit.api.element.ListView<T>
Type Parameters:
T - the item type
All Implemented Interfaces:
PanelElement
public final class ListView<T> extends AbstractPanelElement
A list whose rows follow the consumer's data while the screen is open (7.3.0): one row element per item, added, removed and reordered as the items change, each row kept for as long as its item's key is in the list. 
ListView.<Sandbox>builder()
        .items(() -> sandboxes.list())                       // read every frame; the data is yours
        .key(Sandbox::id)                                    // stable identity across refreshes
        .row(s -> sandboxRow(s))                             // one row element per item
        .selection(() -> selectedId, id -> selectedId = id)  // optional: one selected key
        .gap(2)
        .empty(TextLabel.builder().text(Component.literal("No sandboxes yet")).build())
        .build();

Keyed rows

Every frame the list reads items() and compares its keys with the last ones (cheap: nothing is built when they are the same). A new key gets a row from the factory, attached to the screen at once, exactly as an element present at the screen's init is (Attachment: a text field builds its EditBox, a button registers its focus stand-in). A key that is gone has its row detached: focus it held is let go, its stand-ins leave the screen, an open popover closes. A key that stays keeps its row, the same instance, so a rename field keeps its text and focus and a key button stays in capture while the data refreshes. Rows are in the order of items(). Two items with the same key show one row, the first.

A row is built from the item as it was when its key first appeared. What a row shows that can change (a name, a count) it reads through a supplier from your data, by key, as every MenuKit element reads its value.

Rows are ordinary elements

A row is any AbstractPanelElement, usually a Flow, so the list can place it: rows are stacked top to bottom, gap apart, each given the list's whole width, a hidden row taking no room. They are drawn, hit-tested, claimed and made inert like any child, through ChildDispatch, and they draw for the kind of screen they are on. A row that changes height (a Flow child that hides or shows, a Section that opens) moves the rows below it on the next frame: the rows are placed from their heights every frame. A row that is a Section keeps its open state for as long as its key, through renames and refreshes, so a list of sections expands in place with no more API.

Height follows the rows

Its height is its rows', read every frame, so a ScrollContainer around it scrolls it, its range changing as rows come and go. A list longer than its room belongs in one: put the list in a ScrollContainer.builder().fillHeight() under a fixed header, and only the list scrolls.

A list in the middle of a page pushes what is below it (7.3.0): it reports its whole height, the toolbar it draws included, as growth (extraLayoutHeight()), so place the elements after it as if the list took no room, as after a closed Section. A panel, a Tabs page (with or without a filling element), a Section's content, a Column or Row and a Flow then move them down as rows are added or grow, and up as they go, in the same frame.

Selection: the consumer's, by key

With selection(get, set), one key is selected, held by you (a lens, read every frame). A click on a row where none of its controls takes the click selects it (with the toolbar's remove or arrows, any click in a row does, its control acting too); a row reads your field to show its actions only while selected (visibleWhen(() -> id.equals(selectedId))). The selected row reads clearly in both looks: in the Default look a one-pixel outline, white while the list has the keyboard, gray otherwise; in the Panel look a card row (a boxed Flow) is washed lighter inside its border, and any other row is outlined. After a click in the list, Up and Down move the selection (not while a text field has the keys). When the selection changes other than by a click (your code selecting a new item, the arrow keys), the list asks the scroll area around it to bring the selected row into view (PanelElement.takeRevealRequest()). A selected key whose item is gone clears the selection: set(null).

Empty

empty(element) is shown, in the list's place, while items() is empty.

Editing (7.3.0)

Every option below is optional, and a list with none of them is the list above, exactly. The data stays yours: the list only calls back, and shows what items() returns next, so a refused add or move (a cap, a rule) changes nothing and there is nothing to undo. 
ListView.<LockGroup>builder()
    .items(groups::all).key(LockGroup::id).row(this::groupRow)
    .add(Component.literal("+ Slot group"), () -> groups.addSlotGroup())   // one button per kind
    .add(Component.literal("+ Item group"),
         Component.literal("Locks that follow an item"), () -> groups.addItemGroup())   // with a tooltip
    .remove(id -> groups.delete(id))                                       // removes the selected row
    .confirmRemove(g -> Component.literal("Delete " + g.name() + "?"))     // asks first
    .move((id, toIndex) -> groups.move(id, toIndex))                       // moves the selected row
    .pinned(LockGroup::isDefault)                                          // can't be removed or moved
    .build();
  • Add (ListView.Builder.add(Component, Supplier)): one button per kind in the list's toolbar. The action returns the new item's key, or null and the list finds the key that appeared; either way the new row is scrolled into view, and a search query that would hide it is cleared. A tooltip between the label and the action, fixed or read while hovered, says what the kind is. ListView.Builder.addDisabledWhen(BooleanSupplier) grays them.
  • Remove (ListView.Builder.remove): a "- Remove item" button right of the add buttons, acting on the selected row; it can take its own label and tooltip. ListView.Builder.removeDisabledWhen(BooleanSupplier) grays it, and every row's cross with controlsInRows (a list at its minimum length). ListView.Builder.confirmRemove asks first, in a ConfirmDialog whose body names the item, read when it shows. Once the row is gone the row that took its place is selected (the one before it when it was last), so a second click removes the next.
  • Move (ListView.Builder.move): up and down buttons after remove, moving the selected row one place. toIndex is the place in items(). With the list's keyboard, Alt+Up and Alt+Down do the same.
  • Pinned (ListView.Builder.pinned): those rows can't be removed or moved, and no other row moves past them. Their order is still yours.
  • Disabled, with a reason (ListView.Builder.disabledReason): while the list's own disabledWhen holds, the reason shows above the grayed rows.
  • Search (ListView.Builder.search(Function)) and sort (ListView.Builder.sort(Component, Comparator)): in the toolbar, the search field on the left taking the free width, the sort picker and its direction after it. Search is case-insensitive "contains" on the item's text; "No matches" shows when nothing does, distinct from empty. A selected row the query hides stays selected. Two or more sorts get a picker ("Sort: Name") and a direction button (an arrow beside bars, its tooltip "Ascending" or "Descending"; a click flips it); the first is the default. A list can't both sort and move: build() throws.

Remove, up and down are grayed while nothing is selected or the selected row can't do it: a pinned row, up on the top row and down on the bottom one, a move next to a pinned row, remove on a row a query hides, and either arrow while a query is typed (a move in a filtered view would land somewhere you can't see). Without ListView.Builder.selection(Supplier, Consumer) the list keeps its own selection for them.

The toolbar

Search, sort, add, remove and the arrows sit in one toolbar the list makes, toolbar(), in that order from the left: an ordinary element you place above the list's scroll area, so it stays put while the rows scroll. It lines up with the edges of whatever it is laid out in: placed by you, it is as wide as its container gives it, like any other element, so beside a scroll area as wide as the page its right end is the scroll area's outer edge (past the scrollbar and the band's inset), level with the controls above it. Place it the rows' gap above the scroll area so it reads as part of the list. A list whose toolbar you never ask for draws it at its own top, that gap above the rows, as wide as the rows (inside the band and clear of the scrollbar), and it scrolls with them. It grays with the list.

ListView.Builder.title puts the list's heading on the toolbar's line, at its left edge, so a heading and its buttons share one line instead of the heading sitting alone above them: 

ListView.<Range>builder()
    .items(ranges::all).key(Range::id).row(this::rangeRow)
    .title(() -> Component.literal("Range counts  ")                   // read every frame
            .append(Component.literal(ranges.size() + " rows")
                    .withColor(look.textColor(TextRole.MUTED))))         // the screen's look, its gray
    .add(Component.literal("+ Add range"), () -> ranges.add())
    .build();
The title reads, left to right, before the search field (which then takes the width between them) or before empty room up to the buttons. It is drawn in the heading style a Section's title has for the look, centered on the buttons' line as a label in a crossAlign(CENTER) Flow is, and grays with the list. A supplier is read every frame, so a live count changes in place; a title too long for the line is cut with "..." before the search field or the first button, its styles kept, and shown whole in a tooltip. A title can carry a hover tooltip of its own, title(title, tooltip) (a config option's description, say), fixed or read while hovered as a button's is; it shows instead, cut or not, as a Section with a tooltip does. A list with a title and nothing else for a toolbar has one all the same: the title's line. Without a title the toolbar is as above, exactly.

Controls in each row, for small lists

ListView.Builder.controlsInRows() puts up, down and a remove cross in every row instead, for a short list where each row is its own thing to edit (a config list of text fields): no selection needed. They sit on the row's first line at its trailing edge, after a vertical divider line: inside a boxed Flow's card, on a Section's header line (what opens under it keeps the whole width), or, for any other row (a bare text field), beside it with the same divider. Each keeps its slot whether or not it shows (a pinned row has none), so they line up down the list. Add stays in the toolbar.

The row is yours

The list draws nothing in a row but the selection and, with controlsInRows, its controls. Your own controls in a row (a toggle, an Edit button that opens an EditDialog) go where your row puts them: in a row Flow after a Flow.spacer() they sit at its right end, and Flow.Builder.crossAlign centers them on the line.

    • toolbar

      public PanelElement toolbar()
      The toolbar: the title, search, sort, add, and remove and the arrows, whichever the list has, an ordinary element to put above the list's scroll area so it stays put while the rows scroll. Once this is called the list leaves the toolbar to you; a list whose toolbar is never asked for draws it at its own top, above the rows (it then scrolls with them). The same element every call.

      IllegalStateException - when the list has nothing for a toolbar: no title, no add, no search, fewer than two sorts, and no remove or move outside the rows

    • screenKind

      public void screenKind(ScreenKind kind)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      The kind of screen the owning panel is on, handed down whenever it changes, before the next layout pass. For an element whose size depends on the kind (a Tabs insets its body on a Default-look screen's page), so it measures for the screen it is on from the first frame. An element holding others passes it on to them (a ScrollContainer in a Tabs body sizes its band's inset by it). Default: no-op.

    • inDialog

      public void inDialog(boolean inDialog)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Whether the owning panel is a dialog (a modal, Panel.tracksAsModal) rather than part of the screen, handed down when that is set (7.2.0). On an Default-look screen a list band (a ScrollContainer's, a Tabs page) insets its content by the full screen's ScrollContainer.DEFAULT_INSET_X and ScrollContainer.DEFAULT_INSET_Y; inside a dialog the frame and its padding are already the margin, so a band insets by the dialog's own gap, ScrollContainer.DIALOG_INSET, instead. An element holding others passes it on to them. Default: no-op.

    • inBand

      public void inBand(boolean inBand)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Whether the element sits on a list band another element draws (7.3.0): a Tabs page whose body fills it (PanelElement.fillHeight(int)). There a ScrollContainer draws no band of its own (no second background, no separators, no second inset), only its scrollbar, so the page looks the same whichever side scrolls. Handed down before layout; an element holding others passes it on to them. Default: no-op.

    • renderCulled

      public void renderCulled(RenderContext ctx)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Called each frame instead of PanelElement.render(RenderContext) for a visible element that is skipped only because its box lies wholly outside the clip in play (7.4.0): a row scrolled out of a ScrollContainer, a list's row past its scroll area, a section of the container region out of view. The element is still shown, just not on screen, so it can mark its state as held rather than gone: a slot element keeps its slot parked instead of handing it back to the menu's layout, as it would for a hidden one. Never called for a hidden element (its own PanelElement.isVisible() false, or a hidden or collapsed parent): that one gets neither call.

      An element that contains others forwards it to its shown children (ChildDispatch.renderCulled(List, RenderContext)), so a culled section reaches the slots inside it. The context is the one PanelElement.render(RenderContext) would have had. Default: no-op.

    • renderOverlay

      public void renderOverlay(RenderContext ctx)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Second-pass render for transient overlays that draw outside the element's layout bounds (a Dropdown's popover). Runs after every element's PanelElement.render(RenderContext), so an overlay is always on top regardless of declaration order. Pairs with PanelElement.getActiveOverlayBounds(InputContext), the input side. Default: no-op.

      public void onAttach(net.minecraft.client.gui.screens.Screen screen)
      Description copied from interface: PanelElement
      Screen-attach lifecycle hook, called when the containing screen reaches its init(). Elements that wrap vanilla widgets register them here so vanilla's focus, keyboard and narration reach them. Default: no-op.

      Screen-detach lifecycle hook, the mirror of PanelElement.onAttach(Screen). Default: no-op.
